blocks.text: 1. Hidden Markov Models

blocks.alt: A hidden state produces an observed emission and moves to the next hidden state

blocks.text: Bayesian Networks, the previous topic, represented dependencies between variables at a single, fixed point, a snapshot of how different quantities relate to each other. Hidden Markov Models apply that same probabilistic, Bayes-theorem-grounded reasoning specifically to sequential, ordered data, exactly the kind of temporally structured data already emphasized throughout the entire Time Series Machine Learning module.

Hidden Markov Models introduce a genuinely different structural idea beyond ordinary sequential modeling, however: some variables in the model are hidden, meaning they are never directly observed or measured at all, only inferred indirectly from other, genuinely observable variables that depend on them.
2. Hidden versus Observed Variables

blocks.alt: A hidden variable is not directly seen while an observed variable is

blocks.text: An observed variable is one directly measured or recorded in the actual data, the specific words spoken in an audio recording, or the specific symptoms a patient actually reports. A hidden variable, by contrast, represents some true underlying state that genuinely exists but is never directly measured at all, only inferred from its effects on the observed variables.

A classic example makes this concrete: the actual grammatical part of speech behind a given word, noun, verb, adjective, is a hidden variable, since a written or spoken word does not come with an explicit label announcing its grammatical role, only the observed word itself is directly available. The entire core modeling challenge a Hidden Markov Model addresses is inferring this genuinely hidden sequence of states purely from the sequence of observed variables that were actually generated by it.
3. The Markov Property

blocks.alt: The current state determines the next state while distant past states are irrelevant

blocks.text: Hidden Markov Models rely on a specific, deliberate simplification called the Markov Property, which states that the next hidden state depends only on the current hidden state, not on the entire history of every earlier hidden state that came before it. This directly connects back to the temporal, order-respecting discipline already emphasized throughout Time Series Split in the Cross Validation module, though the Markov Property goes further, deliberately limiting how much of the past actually matters for predicting the future.

This is a deliberate simplification, philosophically similar in spirit to Naive Bayes's own independence assumption already covered in depth in its own topic, trading away some genuine realism, since real sequences often do depend on more than just the immediately preceding state, in exchange for real, substantial mathematical tractability, since modeling dependence on the entire history directly would quickly become computationally intractable for any sequence of meaningful length.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: The name Markov comes directly from this specific property, honoring the mathematician who first formalized it. This same Markov Property underlies a broad family of models across probability theory and machine learning, Hidden Markov Models being just one well-known member of that family.

blocks.text: 4. The Two-Layer Structure

blocks.alt: A hidden state layer sits beneath an observed emission layer

blocks.text: A Hidden Markov Model is built from two connected layers. The first layer is a hidden Markov chain: at every single time step, there is one hidden state, and that hidden state depends only on the hidden state at the immediately preceding time step, exactly the Markov Property covered in the previous section. The second layer is the sequence of actual observations, one emitted at every time step, with each observation depending only on that specific time step's hidden state.

Two sets of probabilities fully describe this two-layer structure. Transition probabilities specify how likely the model is to move from one particular hidden state to another between consecutive time steps. Emission probabilities specify how likely a given hidden state is to actually produce, or emit, a particular observed value. Together, these two probability structures completely define how the hidden chain evolves and how it generates the observed sequence that a Hidden Markov Model actually gets trained and evaluated on.

blocks.text: 5. Three Classic Problems

Hidden Markov Models are traditionally used to solve three distinct classic problems. The evaluation problem asks, given a fully specified model and an observed sequence, how likely is this specific observed sequence to have actually occurred under this model overall, useful for comparing how well different candidate models fit the same observed data.

The decoding problem asks, given a fully specified model and an observed sequence, what is the single most likely hidden state sequence that actually produced it, covered in depth in the next section through the Viterbi Algorithm. The learning problem asks, given only a collection of observed sequences with no known hidden states or probabilities at all, what transition and emission probabilities best explain those observations, the model-fitting problem underlying training a Hidden Markov Model from raw data in the first place.
6. The Viterbi Algorithm

blocks.alt: An observed sequence runs through the Viterbi algorithm to find the most likely hidden path

blocks.text: Solving the decoding problem, finding the single most likely hidden state sequence behind a given observed sequence, naively requires checking every single possible hidden sequence directly, a number that grows exponentially with sequence length and becomes hopelessly intractable for any sequence of meaningful, realistic length.

The Viterbi Algorithm provides an efficient, exact shortcut around this exponential explosion, building up the best possible hidden sequence step by step, reusing partial computation already done for earlier time steps rather than recomputing everything from scratch for every candidate sequence. This lets the Viterbi Algorithm find the single genuinely most likely hidden sequence in a computational cost that grows only linearly with sequence length, rather than exponentially, without ever needing to check every possible sequence directly one by one.
7. Connecting Back to Time Series Machine Learning

blocks.alt: Time series machine learning extends into hidden Markov models

blocks.text: It is worth connecting this directly back to the entire Time Series Machine Learning module, covered earlier in this course, since Hidden Markov Models are built specifically for sequential, temporally ordered data, exactly the same fundamental data structure that module addressed throughout its own topics.

Hidden Markov Models are, however, a genuinely different kind of tool from the forecasting models already covered in that earlier module, focused specifically on inferring a sequence of discrete, hidden states from observed data, rather than directly forecasting future continuous numeric values the way most time series forecasting techniques do. Both families of technique share the same underlying respect for chronological, sequential structure, but they solve genuinely different kinds of problems within that shared domain.
8. Classic Applications

blocks.alt: Hidden Markov models power speech recognition and part of speech tagging

blocks.text: Speech recognition is one of the most classic, historically significant Hidden Markov Model applications: the hidden states represent the words or phonemes actually intended by the speaker, while the observed variables are the raw, continuous audio signal actually captured by a microphone, and the model's job is inferring the intended words purely from that raw audio.

Part-of-speech tagging is another classic application, already previewed in this topic's earlier example: hidden states represent each word's true grammatical role, while observed variables are the actual words written in a sentence. Gene sequence analysis offers a third classic application, where hidden states represent functionally meaningful regions of a gene, while observed variables are the raw DNA sequence itself, letters representing individual nucleotides.

blocks.text: 9. When Hidden Markov Models Are the Right Choice

Hidden Markov Models are the right choice specifically for sequential data with a genuine, meaningful underlying state that is never directly observed itself, speech, natural language, and biological sequences all being classic, well-established examples already covered in this topic, where inferring that hidden state from observable evidence is the actual, central modeling goal.

They fit especially well when the Markov Property, covered earlier in this topic, is a reasonable enough approximation for the problem at hand, situations where recent history genuinely matters far more than distant history in determining what comes next. When genuinely long-range dependencies matter a great deal, situations where the Markov Property badly misrepresents the true underlying structure of the data, modern deep learning sequence models, built specifically to capture longer-range dependencies than the Markov Property allows, are usually the better, more capable modern choice instead.
10. Worked Example
The example below fits a Hidden Markov Model to a simple sequence of observations, then uses the Viterbi Algorithm to decode the most likely hidden state sequence behind it.

code.content:
import numpy as np
from hmmlearn import hmm

# Two hidden states: "Rainy" (0) and "Sunny" (1)
# Three observations: "Walk" (0), "Shop" (1), "Clean" (2)
model = hmm.CategoricalHMM(n_components=2, random_state=42)

# Manually specify a plausible model (normally learned from data instead)
model.startprob_ = np.array([0.6, 0.4])         # prior probability of starting Rainy vs Sunny
model.transmat_ = np.array([[0.7, 0.3],          # transition probabilities
                             [0.4, 0.6]])
model.emissionprob_ = np.array([[0.1, 0.4, 0.5],  # emission probabilities per hidden state
                                 [0.6, 0.3, 0.1]])

# An observed sequence: Walk, Shop, Clean, Walk
observed_sequence = np.array([[0, 1, 2, 0]]).T

log_probability, hidden_states = model.decode(observed_sequence, algorithm="viterbi")
state_names = ["Rainy", "Sunny"]
print("Most likely hidden weather sequence:", [state_names[s] for s in hidden_states])
print(f"Log probability of this hidden sequence: {log_probability:.3f}")

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: model.decode with algorithm="viterbi" runs exactly the Viterbi Algorithm covered in this topic, efficiently finding the single most likely hidden state sequence without ever checking every possible sequence directly.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Hidden Markov Models apply probabilistic, Bayesian reasoning to sequential data, with some variables genuinely hidden, never directly observed.
The Markov Property assumes the next hidden state depends only on the current one, not the entire history, trading realism for tractability.
The model has two layers: a hidden Markov chain and an observation layer, linked by transition and emission probabilities.
Three classic problems: evaluation, how likely a sequence is; decoding, the most likely hidden sequence; learning, fitting the probabilities from data.
The Viterbi Algorithm efficiently solves decoding, avoiding the exponential cost of checking every possible hidden sequence directly.
It addresses the same sequential data theme as the Time Series Machine Learning module, but solves a genuinely different kind of problem.
Classic applications include speech recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and gene sequence analysis.
It fits sequential data with a genuine hidden state and a reasonable Markov Property approximation; long-range dependencies favor deep learning instead.
